unit.title: Exchange rates and the balance of payments

sections.title: Consequences of changes in exchange rates

linked_units.why: current account deficits/surpluses, exchange rate systems compared, Marshall-Lerner and J-curve (HL)
interest rates as a tool to defend a currency

unit.exam_weight: Highest share of HL marks M22–N25 (10.6%), in all 8 sessions. Exchange rate diagram asked 21 times.

source.questions: original (written for Onside; fictional countries and data)

note_corrections.issue: Notes say 'more quantity of dollars is traded'. With demand shifting left along an upward-sloping supply curve, the quantity traded falls.

Notes say exports rise because 'the currency is less expensive'. The mechanism is that the country's goods become relatively cheaper, which raises foreign demand for its exports and so for its currency.

concepts.definition: The value of one currency expressed in terms of another.
Exchange rates set by demand and supply in the foreign exchange market, with no central bank intervention.
A rise in the value of a currency in a floating system.
A fall in the value of a currency in a floating system.

concepts.term: Causes of changes in currency demand
concepts.definition: Foreign demand for exports (goods, services, tourism), relative inflation, relative growth, inward FDI and portfolio investment, relative interest rates, inward remittances, speculation, central bank buying.

concepts.term: Causes of changes in currency supply
concepts.definition: Domestic demand for imports, relative inflation and growth, outward FDI and portfolio investment, relative interest rates, outward remittances, speculation, central bank selling.
Financial investment such as buying stocks and bonds.
Investment by multinational corporations in productive facilities.
Money sent home by workers living and earning abroad.
Buying and selling currencies to profit from expected exchange rate changes.
Converting prices between currencies, finding the inverse rate, and percentage change in a currency's value.
Effects on net exports, demand-pull and cost-push inflation, growth, unemployment, current account, foreign debt and living standards.
The central bank sets the exchange rate and intervenes to keep it there.
Using reserves, changing interest rates, borrowing abroad, limiting imports.
A government decision to lower / raise a fixed exchange rate.
Mostly floating, with periodic central bank intervention to smooth sharp swings; includes pegs within a band.
A currency held above / below its free-market equilibrium value.
A record of all transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world over a period; credits equal debits.
Balance of trade in goods + balance of trade in services + net income + net current transfers.
Capital transfers + transactions in non-produced, non-financial assets.
Net FDI + net portfolio investment + reserve assets + official borrowing.
The accounts sum to zero, so a current account deficit is matched by a capital plus financial account surplus.

diagram_checklists.name: Exchange rate diagram: floating rate change
items: Vertical axis: price of the currency in another currency (e.g. USD per VLD)
Horizontal axis: quantity of the currency
Downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, both labelled
Initial equilibrium rate and quantity marked (e1, Q1)
Correct curve shifts in the correct direction, with new curve labelled
New equilibrium rate marked (e2) and higher/lower than e1 as the cause requires
Written link: the cause → demand or supply of the currency → appreciation or depreciation
common_errors: Shifting demand when the cause works through supply (e.g. imports)
Axis labelled only 'Price' with no currency pair
Showing the other currency's market without saying so

diagram_checklists.name: Exchange rate diagram: defending a fixed rate
items: Axes labelled as for a floating diagram
Fixed exchange rate shown as a horizontal line and labelled
Shift that creates pressure (e.g. demand falls) shown and labelled
Excess supply (or excess demand) at the fixed rate identified
Central bank action shown: buying its own currency with foreign reserves shifts demand back to the right (for upward pressure the opposite: selling its own currency shifts supply right)
Rate stays at the fixed level; written link explains the action
common_errors: Central bank sells its own currency to stop a fall
Rate drawn as moving despite intervention
No mention of reserves or interest rates

diagram_checklists.name: AD/AS diagram: effect of depreciation
items: Vertical axis: average price level; horizontal axis: real GDP
AD shifts right (net exports rise) — and/or SRAS shifts left if imported inputs matter
New price level and real GDP marked
Written link: depreciation → exports cheaper, imports dearer → (X−M) rises → AD rises
common_errors: Forgetting cost-push via imported inputs in evaluation

questions.prompt: Country A has a floating exchange rate. Which change is most likely to cause the currency of Country A to appreciate?

options.text: The central bank of Country A lowers interest rates relative to other countries.
options.misconception: Lower relative interest rates attract less financial capital, so demand for the currency falls.

options.text: Inflation in Country A rises faster than in its trading partners.
options.misconception: Higher relative inflation makes exports less competitive, lowering currency demand and raising supply.

options.text: Multinational firms increase their investment in factories in Country A.
Residents of Country A take more holidays abroad.
options.misconception: Spending abroad is an import of services, which increases the supply of the domestic currency.

hints: Ask which option makes foreigners need more of Country A's currency.
Inward FDI means foreign firms must buy the currency to pay for buildings and workers. Check what each other option does to demand or supply.
questions.targets: Direction of demand vs supply factors

questions.prompt: The currency of Country B depreciates sharply. Country B imports most of its oil. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: The value of Country B's foreign-currency debt falls.
options.misconception: Depreciation raises the domestic-currency cost of debt held in foreign currency.

options.text: Cost-push inflation, as imported inputs become more expensive.
Net exports fall because exports become more expensive abroad.
Living standards rise because imports become cheaper.
options.misconception: Imports become more expensive after a depreciation.

hints: Think about what happens to the price of imports in the domestic currency.
Oil is an input for most firms. Which curve on the AD/AS diagram shifts when input costs rise?

questions.prompt: Country C fixes its exchange rate. Demand for its exports falls, putting downward pressure on the currency. What should the central bank do to keep the fixed rate?

options.text: Sell its own currency and buy foreign currency.
options.misconception: Selling its own currency adds supply and pushes the value down further.

options.text: Buy its own currency using foreign currency reserves.

options.misconception: Lower rates reduce financial inflows and weaken the currency.
Higher spending raises incomes and imports, adding currency supply; it does not defend the rate directly.

hints: At the fixed rate there is now excess supply of the currency. What removes it?
The central bank needs to add demand for its own currency. What does it pay with?

questions.prompt: Country D has a current account deficit of $20 billion and a capital account balance of zero. Ignoring errors and omissions, its financial account must be:

options.misconception: Treats accounts as moving together rather than offsetting.
Forgets that the whole balance of payments sums to zero.

options.text: impossible to know without trade data

hints: All the accounts together must add up to zero.
Current + capital + financial = 0. Put in the numbers you know.

questions.prompt: If €1 = $1.25, what is the value of $1 in euros?

options.misconception: Uses the same number without inverting.
Guesses a nearby value without calculating.

hints: You need the inverse of the rate.
Divide 1 by 1.25.

marking_points: Financial investment (e.g. buying shares/stocks or bonds) [1]
Made across borders / in another country, without control of a productive facility [1]
questions.model_answer_note: An accurate definition covering both points earns 2; a vague or partly correct one earns 1.
hints: Which account does it belong to, and how is it different from FDI?
Name what is bought, and say where the investor is.

marking_points: A currency whose exchange rate is higher [1]
than its free-market equilibrium value (often held there by government or central bank action) [1]
hints: Compare the actual rate with what the market alone would set.
Higher or lower than equilibrium?
questions.targets: Asked in M23 P3 and N25 P2

questions.prompt: In January 1 bola = 2.40 zeds. In December 1 bola = 2.10 zeds. Calculate the percentage change in the value of (i) the bola and (ii) the zed between January and December.
hints: Percentage change = (new − old) / old × 100. For the zed, first find the value of 1 zed in bolas.
The two answers are not the same size. Invert both rates before comparing.
questions.targets: Trap: a 12.5% fall is not a 12.5% rise for the other currency

questions.prompt: A firm in Kuva sells a machine for 50 000 kuvars (KVR). The exchange rate changes from US$1 = KVR 40 to US$1 = KVR 50. Calculate the change in the US$ price of the machine.
hints: Convert the KVR price into US$ at each rate.
More KVR per dollar means the KVR has depreciated. Should the US$ price go up or down?

questions.prompt: Balance of payments for Country Lira (US$ billion): exports of goods 120; imports of goods 150; exports of services 45; imports of services 30; net income −8; net current transfers +11; capital account +2; net FDI +15; net portfolio investment −6; official borrowing +3; reserve assets ?. (a) Calculate the current account balance. [2] (b) Calculate the value of reserve assets. [2]
marking_points: (b) financial account = +10 or equivalent working [1], reserve assets = −2 [1]
hints: List which items belong to the current account and which to the financial account.
The three accounts sum to zero. Find the financial account first, then solve for the missing item.
questions.targets: Account membership + BoP identity (P2/P3 calc pattern)

questions.prompt: Using an exchange rate diagram, explain how a large rise in the number of foreign tourists visiting Veld is likely to affect the value of the veld (VLD).

marking.diagram_must_show: Demand for VLD shifts right; exchange rate rises from e1 to e2
marking.explanation_must_include: Tourism is an export of services; foreign tourists must buy VLD to spend in Veld; demand for VLD rises; the VLD appreciates

hints: Is spending by foreign tourists an export or an import for Veld? Which curve does that affect?
Tourists need VLD to pay for hotels. Show that on the demand side and mark the new rate.

questions.prompt: Using an exchange rate diagram, explain how the central bank of Ostra could maintain its fixed exchange rate after a fall in demand for Ostra's exports.

marking.diagram_must_show: Fixed rate line; demand shifts left creating excess supply at the fixed rate; central bank buying shifts demand back to restore the fixed rate
marking.explanation_must_include: Lower export demand reduces demand for the currency; the central bank uses foreign reserves to buy its currency (or raises interest rates) so demand returns and the rate stays fixed

hints: What gap appears at the fixed rate after demand falls?
The central bank must create extra demand for its own currency. What does it use to pay?

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to show how a rise in interest rates in Country E, relative to other countries, affects its current account. One step does not belong.

steps.text: Interest rates in Country E rise relative to other countries
Foreign savers move funds into Country E's bank deposits and bonds
Demand for Country E's currency rises
Exports become more expensive abroad and imports become cheaper
Net exports fall and the current account balance worsens
Foreign demand for Country E's exports rises

hints: Start with the financial flow, not trade.
Interest rates change the currency first; the currency then changes trade. One step points the wrong way.
questions.targets: Chain from interest rates to current account

questions.prompt: Explain how a fall in interest rates in a country, relative to its trading partners, is likely to affect its exchange rate and its current account balance.

marking.rubric: Jin's DEEDE without evaluation: definitions, explanation of the chain, a labelled exchange rate diagram, clear link to the current account
key_content: Define exchange rate, depreciation, current account
Lower relative rates reduce the return on deposits and bonds; financial capital flows out
Demand for the currency falls and/or supply rises
Exchange rate diagram: D left and/or S right, rate falls e1 → e2
Depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer; net exports rise; current account improves (after a time lag)
marking.reference: Compare with the P1 (a) 10-mark bands in any M22–N25 P1 mark scheme

hints: There are two stages: interest rates → currency, then currency → trade.
Show the capital outflow on the exchange rate diagram, then explain what the new rate does to X and M.

questions.prompt: Using real-world examples, evaluate the effects of a sustained depreciation of a country's currency on different stakeholders.

marking.rubric: Jin's DEEDE: define, explain, diagram, example, evaluate
key_content: Exporters: cheaper abroad, more sales and jobs
Import-competing firms: imports dearer, domestic demand shifts to them
Consumers: dearer imports, lower real incomes, higher cost of living
Firms using imported inputs: higher costs, cost-push inflation (SRAS left)
Government/firms with foreign-currency debt: debt burden rises
Workers: more jobs in export sectors if AD rises; risk of job losses if cost-push dominates
evaluation_angles: Price elasticity of exports and imports (links to Marshall-Lerner, unit 17)
Short run vs long run (J-curve, unit 17)
Where the economy is in the business cycle (demand-pull risk near potential output)
Share of imported inputs in production
marking.reference: Compare with the P1 (b) 15-mark bands in any M22–N25 P1 mark scheme

plan_prompts: Define depreciation and one more key term
List at least three stakeholders and the effect on each
Which diagram (exchange rate or AD/AS) and what it shows
One real-world example and what happened
Your judgement: who gains most, who loses most, and what it depends on
hints: Group stakeholders into winners and losers before writing.
For evaluation, ask what the effect depends on: elasticities, time period, imported inputs, foreign debt.
questions.targets: P1 Q3 (b) style; related past essays on appreciation/depreciation consequences
